problem: The asymmetric beam direction is reversed. In a left-hand-drive country the driver sits on the left and traffic runs on the right, so the kerb (near side) is on the right; the beam must rise on the right and stay low and short on the left, towards oncoming traffic. The text says it is low on the right in left-hand-drive countries while also claiming this lights the near side, which contradicts itself. India drives on the left, so Indian lamps are mirrored again.
fix: The beam pattern is asymmetric: it is low and short on the left in left-hand-drive countries (traffic keeps right), so the beam dips toward oncoming traffic and rises on the near side to light the kerb without glare. In India, where traffic keeps left, the pattern is mirrored: the dip is on the right.

problem: The question fixes the reflector as the same for both lamps, but the answer explains the difference by saying the halogen beam may be narrower. With the same reflector the beam shape is essentially the same, so the real reason the 1500 lm halogen looks brighter is simply that it puts about 1.5 times the flux into the same beam. The given answer does not answer the question as posed.
fix: Keep the question and change the answer to: with the same reflector the beam shape is similar, so the halogen's 1500 lm gives about 1.5 times the illuminance (lux) of the 1000 lm LED; efficacy sets the current drawn, not the light on the road. Alternatively reword the question so the two lamps use different reflectors, and keep the narrower-beam explanation.
